explanation: `obj` has one own property, `name`, so `Object.keys` returns one key. `greet` isn't copied onto `obj`. Lookup finds it on `base`, so `obj.greet` is the same function as `base.greet`. The tempting `1 false` assumes inherited methods are copied rather than shared.

`child.n += 1` reads the inherited `0`, then assigns `1` as an own property of `child`, which shadows the parent's value and leaves `parent.n` at `0`. `child.list.push` never assigns to `list`, so it mutates the shared array that `parent` owns. The lesson is that numbers get shadowed on write, but objects are shared through the chain.

`Child`'s fields are initialized after `super()` returns. While `Base`'s constructor is running, `Child.prototype.compute` is already the method being called, but `this.base` doesn't exist yet, so it reads `undefined`. The value `1` would come from `Base.prototype.compute`, which `Child` overrides, so it never runs.

The field is private, so it doesn't appear in `Object.keys`. The `in` operator checks for a string property named `secret`, and the private field is named `#secret` in a separate namespace, so `"secret" in` is `false`. Private fields are invisible to reflection and to any string-keyed check.

The `get` trap runs for every read through the proxy. For `a`, the key exists, so the handler returns `1`. For `b`, the trap returns the fallback string `"missing"`. The option `1 undefined` is what you'd get without the proxy, which shows the trap really did run.

`Reflect.set` returns a boolean instead of throwing. A frozen object refuses the write, so `Reflect.set` returns `false`, and `frozen.n` still holds `1`. Plain assignment would also fail, but in sloppy mode it does so silently, which is why `Reflect` is the clearer way to test a write.

Calling a generator function returns a generator object and doesn't run the body. `created` prints first. The body runs only when `it.next()` is called, and then `started` prints before the `yield` pauses it. Calling `gen()` is lazy, which is what makes generators good for infinite or expensive sequences.
